notes.content:
**Nationalism** = great **love for one's motherland** and the **desire to free it from foreign rule**.

The late 19th and early 20th centuries saw nationalist feelings grow → birth of the **Indian national movement** → **Indian National Congress (1885)**.

**Factors — remember 'RPWEPTRL + Ilbert'**
1. **R**evolt of 1857
2. **P**olitical unification
3. **W**estern education
4. **E**nglish language
5. **P**ress and literature (+ rediscovery of the past)
6. **T**ransport and communication
7. **R**acial discrimination
8. **L**ytton's repressive policies
9. **Immediate cause:** Ilbert Bill controversy

**Revolt of 1857:** failed, but created the idea of **unity and sacrifice**; the feeling of **one nation**; **martyrs** became household names.

**Political unification:** British conquests created a **centralised government** with **uniform laws** for the whole country → feeling of belonging to one nation.

**Western education:** meant to produce **clerks**, but brought ideas of **freedom, liberty, fraternity**; Indians learnt of the **French Revolution** and **American War of Independence**; took **pride in India's past**; rejected the idea that Indians were inferior; educated Indians became **leaders**.

**English language:** a **common language** for educated Indians of different regions → exchange of ideas → **unity**.

notes.subtopic: 3. Press, Literature and Rediscovery of India's Past

fiveW.who: Nationalist editors and writers — Bankim Chandra, Rabindranath Tagore; scholars Cunningham, Jones, Prinsep
fiveW.where: Across India — English and vernacular press
fiveW.what: Newspapers and literature that spread national awareness
fiveW.why: To criticise British policies and create pride in Indian heritage
fiveW.how: Discussed the evils of the Raj and democracy; novels like Anandamath and Ghare Baire

notes.content:
**Press**
• Newspapers in **English and vernacular** languages.
• Leaders used the **vernacular press** to spread modern ideas, discuss **British policies** and the **evils of the Raj**, and the idea of **democracy**.

**Literature**
• **Anandamath** — Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay.
• **Ghare Baire** — Rabindranath Tagore (**first non-European Nobel Prize for Literature, 1913**).

**Rediscovery of the past**
• European scholars **Alexander Cunningham, William Jones, James Prinsep** researched India's heritage.
• Indians rediscovered **Vedic philosophy**, **Chandragupta Maurya**, the **Guptas**, the **Mughals** → **pride and self-confidence** to demand freedom.

**Transport and communication**
• **Lord Dalhousie** and others built **roads and railways**.
• **Regional barriers narrowed**; people met, exchanged ideas and realised they had **common problems and goals**.
• **Victoria Terminus** (now **Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus**) — UNESCO World Heritage Site.

**Racial discrimination**
• British saw Indians as **inferior and uncivilised**; Indians were humiliated.
• **High posts reserved** for the British.
• Indians **barred from railway coaches, hospitals, parks and clubs** meant for Europeans.
• Angered the **educated intelligentsia**, who united the people.

fiveW.what: Delhi Durbar, Vernacular Press Act, Arms Act
fiveW.why: To assert imperial power and suppress criticism
fiveW.how: Lavish Durbar during famine; gagged the Indian press; licences for arms only for Indians

notes.content:
• **Delhi Durbar (1877):** lavish ceremony proclaiming **Queen Victoria Empress of India** — held while **south India suffered a famine** with no relief.
• **Vernacular Press Act (1878):** restrictions on the **Indian-language press**; anything **anti-British forbidden**.
• **Arms Act (1878):** Indians needed a **licence** to carry arms; **Europeans did not** — clear racial discrimination.

**Result:** Indians decided to take **concerted action** against the British.

notes.subtopic: 6. Immediate Cause — The Ilbert Bill Controversy

fiveW.who: Lord Ripon (Viceroy); C.P. Ilbert (Law Member); European community
fiveW.what: Bill allowing Indian judges to try Europeans
fiveW.why: Ripon wanted to remove a racial inequality in law
fiveW.how: Europeans protested violently; the bill was diluted

notes.content:
• **Lord Ripon**, Lytton's successor, tried to address Indian grievances.
• **Ilbert Bill (1883)** by **C.P. Ilbert**, Law Member: **senior Indian magistrates could try Europeans** accused of crimes.
• **Anglo-Indian (European) officials and non-officials opposed it violently** → bill **modified in favour of Europeans**.
• **Lesson for Indians:** they must **organise and fight for their rights** → need for a **political body**.

notes.subtopic: 7. Formation and Objectives of the Indian National Congress

fiveW.who: A.O. Hume (founder); W.C. Bonnerjee (first president); Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Badruddin Tyabji
fiveW.what: Indian National Congress — first all-India political organisation
fiveW.why: A platform to voice Indian grievances and organise public opinion
fiveW.how: First session of about 72 delegates; petitions and resolutions to the government

notes.content:
• **1883** — **Surendranath Banerjee** convened the **Indian National Conference** in Calcutta.
• **1885** — **A.O. Hume** (retired British civil servant) founded the **Indian National Congress**.
• **First session — Bombay (1885)**, president **W.C. Bonnerjee**; attended by **Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Badruddin Tyabji** and others.
• Hume's poem **'An Old Man's Hope'** urged Indians to rise.

**Objectives**
• Promote **friendship and unity** among Indians regardless of race, caste, religion or province.
• **Organise public opinion** on British policies.
• Place **popular demands** before the government.
• Decide the **future course of action**.

At first the Congress was **loyal to the British** — it wanted only **more participation in government**.

questions.answer: Lytton-Press Act · Ripon-Ilbert Bill · Hume-INC · Bonnerjee-President · Banerjee-Conference

questions.question: Define nationalism. State two world events that encouraged nationalism in India.
questions.answer:
• Nationalism: great love for one's motherland and the desire to free it from foreign rule.
  • World events: the French Revolution and the American War of Independence.

questions.question: Although the Revolt of 1857 failed, how did it lead to nationalism?
questions.answer:
• It created the idea of unity and sacrifice for the nation.
  • The feeling of belonging to one nation gained ground as Hindus and Muslims had fought together.
  • Its martyrs (Rani Lakshmibai, Tantia Tope…) became household names and inspired later generations.

questions.question: How did the political unification of India lead to nationalism?
questions.answer: British conquests unified India politically and economically under a centralised government with uniform laws, rules and regulations for the whole country. Living under one system, people began to feel they belonged to one nation.

questions.question: How was the spread of Western education responsible for the rise of nationalism? Was English a factor?
questions.answer:
• Meant to create clerks, it brought ideas of freedom, liberty and fraternity.
  • Indians learnt of the French and American revolutions and dreamed of a free India.
  • They took pride in India's past and rejected the idea of Indian inferiority; many became leaders.
  • Yes — English became a common link language, helping Indians from different regions share ideas and unite.

questions.question: Explain the role of the press and literature in the rise of nationalism.
questions.answer:
• Newspapers in English and vernacular languages discussed British policies, the evils of the Raj and democracy.
  • Nationalist literature — Anandamath (Bankim Chandra) and Ghare Baire (Tagore) — created a cultural awakening and pride in heritage.

questions.question: Name European scholars who revealed India's heritage. How did the rediscovery of the past help nationalism?
questions.answer:
• Alexander Cunningham, William Jones, James Prinsep.
  • Indians rediscovered Vedic philosophy, the wisdom of Chandragupta Maurya, and the glory of the Guptas and Mughals.
  • This gave them pride and self-confidence to demand freedom.

questions.question: How did racial discrimination by the British help the growth of nationalism?
questions.answer:
• The British treated Indians as inferior and uncivilised.
  • High posts were reserved for the British; Indians were barred from railway coaches, hospitals, parks and clubs meant for Europeans.
  • This humiliated the educated intelligentsia, who then united the people against the British.

questions.question: Mention the repressive policies of Lord Lytton.
questions.answer:
• Delhi Durbar (1877) — lavish show to proclaim Queen Victoria Empress of India, during a famine in the south.
  • Vernacular Press Act (1878) — muzzled the Indian-language press.
  • Arms Act (1878) — Indians needed licences for arms; Europeans did not.
questions.topperTip: Always point out the racial bias in the Arms Act — examiners look for it.

questions.question: (Picture) The Viceroy who introduced repressive policies: name him, when appointed, and how he caused nationalism.
questions.answer:
• (a) Lord Lytton.
  • (b) 1876 (Viceroy 1876–80).
  • (c) His Delhi Durbar during famine, Vernacular Press Act and discriminatory Arms Act angered Indians and made them unite for concerted action.

questions.question: What was the Ilbert Bill controversy?
questions.answer:
• In 1883, under Lord Ripon, Law Member C.P. Ilbert introduced a bill allowing senior Indian magistrates to try Europeans.
  • Europeans opposed it violently; it was modified in their favour.
  • Indians realised they must organise to protect their rights — the immediate cause for forming the Congress.

questions.question: Describe the formation and objectives of the Indian National Congress.
questions.answer:
• Founded in 1885 by A.O. Hume; first session at Bombay, presided over by W.C. Bonnerjee, with Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Badruddin Tyabji.
  • Objectives: promote unity among Indians; organise public opinion on British policies; place popular demands before the government; decide the future course of action.
  • Initially loyal — sought more participation in government.
